_about: Hand-run cases for engine 1.7b.10 (2026-11-09). One run per case per app. The opening message is sent verbatim; every later answer comes from the profile card.
rules_for_the_user: Send the opening message exactly as written, as the first message of a new chat in the generation project.
Answer only what the assistant asks, using the card's facts, in a few plain words. Do not volunteer card facts it did not ask about.
If it asks something the card does not cover, answer "No preference."
If the brief gets a card fact wrong, correct it once, in one sentence. Otherwise reply "approved".
Download every file the generation chat gives (the RB) and every file the execution chat gives.
In the execution project, open a new chat, attach the RB, and send it with no text.
Share both conversations (public link) and note the links in the run log.

cases.title: A parent deciding family rules
cases.opening: Is screen time actually bad for kids' brains or is it a moral panic?
card: What you know about the subject
No science background. You know everyday words like "screen time"; terms like "neuroimaging" or "cohort study" are new to you.
To decide your family's rules for tablet and TV: how much, what kind of content, and when.
You have one child, aged 6. You live in France.
Reading on your phone. No length preference.
cases.tests: The situation (child's age) becomes reader context, not a scope restriction; the decision purpose makes the report lead with what the evidence implies for family rules; no personal details in the report. Same question as benchmark topic T3.

cases.title: A talk for colleagues
cases.opening: Do you really need 10,000 steps a day?
card: What you know about the subject
The basics: you read health news, but not research papers.
To prepare a 10-minute talk to your office colleagues and answer their questions afterwards.
You, and you will share it with about 40 office colleagues; they are not health specialists.
Office workers, mostly sitting, aged roughly 25 to 60.
A PDF you can send around. Short enough to read in about 15 minutes.
cases.tests: Readers differ from the requester; the explain-to-others purpose gives reusable explanations and examples; PDF output.

cases.title: An expert checking a claim
cases.opening: Do AI coding assistants actually make experienced developers faster, or does it just feel that way?
card: What you know about the subject
Senior backend developer, 15 years of experience. Comfortable with statistics (effect sizes, confidence intervals, randomised trials).
To check a claim your manager quoted, that AI assistants make developers "55% faster", and to cite the sources back to them.
You, and you will pass it to your manager, who is technical but not a researcher.
Experienced developers working on large existing codebases, not new small projects.
HTML is fine. No length preference.
cases.tests: Expert depth without simplification; the check-and-cite purpose states each conclusion with its exact support and limits; the situation (large existing codebases) as reader context.

cases.title: Everything given upfront
cases.opening: I brief a regional climate committee: they know climate basics but not engineering. I must recommend whether to fund direct-air-capture pilots. PDF, 10 pages max. Can direct air capture of CO2 work at a scale that matters?
card: Already in the opening message. If asked anything else, answer "No preference."
cases.tests: The skip rule: no reader questions, straight to the brief; the page limit.

cases.title: French, no answers
cases.opening: Est-ce que les pompes a chaleur valent le coup dans un climat froid ?
cases.tests: Language (brief, RB and report in French); unanswered points take the defaults and are recorded as assumptions.
